newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Madagascar former ruler back as elected president.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar former ruler back as elected president.

text.p: The proclamation of Didier Ratsiraka as president of Madagascar on Friday crowned his comeback against Albert Zafy, the man who had ended his 16 years as military ruler in a 1993 election.
The 60-year-old former admiral, whose eyesight is failing, is an old master of turnarounds.
As military ruler and virtual dictator he led a socialist revolution in Madagascar in the 1970s before turning to free market reforms and democracy to end an economic slump and popular unrest.
"I have problems seeing, but I am not blind," Ratsiraka reportedly said after fumbling last November to put his ballot through the slot in the box in the first round of the election.
Ratsiraka returned to Madagascar from two years in exile in Paris to run against Zafy, a self-styled populist in a trademark straw hat who led the coalition that ousted him in 1993.
In his successful bid for revenge against Zafy, Ratsiraka campaigned on promises of a "humanistic and ecological" republic in Madagascar, whose 14 million people live in chronic poverty.

A former navy officer who became president under military rule in 1975, Ratsiraka moderated his radical political tone in the years since being known as "the Red Admiral" with his own "Little Red Book".
By 1990, he had formally allowed political opposition parties and in 1992 he made way for a constitution that retained him only as a figurehead president before the elections.
But for the electorate in 1993 the changes were too slow and he lost the last round to Zafy by 33 percent to 67 percent.

Ratsiraka, described by detractors as highly intelligent but aloof, faced opposition as military ruler across the political spectrum, from liberals wanting faster economic reform to leftists accusing him of "wild liberalism".

Austerity programmes he launched in 1982 after prompting from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank revived economic growth and brought a flood of economic aid. By 1990 the government was attracting much-needed foreign investment.
But the effects of the reforms were slow to filter through to most people, who live from farming and exported cash crops.
In the blackest day under his rule, Ratsiraka ordered troops to fire on a huge crowd of protesters on August 10, 1991. The official version was 14 people killed and hundreds wounded.

"He's very clever...most of his problems come from less clever advisors," said an opposition politician at the time. "He sits...putting the nation on computer but he doesn't know what the people are thinking."
Ratsiraka, a slight, good-looking man, was born on November 4, 1936, into a wealthy family at Vatomandry on the east coast and was brought up as a Christian. He remains a fervent Roman Catholic.

He attended a prestigious Jesuit school in Antananarivo and then joined the navy as an officer cadet. He graduated from the Ecole Superieure de Guerre Navale in Paris in 1962, returning to France in 1970 as military attache in the Malagasy embassy.
He was appointed foreign minister in 1972 in the military government headed by General Gabriel Ramanantsoa, who took power when Madagascar's first president resigned after violent demonstrations.
In February 1975, an economic crisis and growing military unrest forced Ramanantsoa to hand over power to Colonel Richard Ratsimandrava, a radical who was assassinated six days later.
Fighting broke out in the army and Ratsiraka, by then a commander in the navy, took charge to restore socialist order.
Married with three daughters, Ratsiraka is reticent about his personal life and remains popular among the very poor.
